headline.funnel_interpretation: Egger’s test is generally not recommended when fewer than 10 studies are available.
headline.results_interpretation: The pooled analysis of 3 studies yielded an overall effect size of 0.95 (95% CI: 0.9–1.0), suggesting that lycopene is associated with a lower risk of bladder cancer. These findings were supported by low between-study heterogeneity (I² = 0.00%), indicating consistent findings across the included studies.

studies.Reference: Are retinol, vitamin C, vitamin E, folate and carotenoids intake associated with bladder cancer risk? Results from the Netherlands Cohort Study.
studies.Authors: Zeegers MP, Goldbohm RA, van den Brandt PA
studies.exposure_measurement_supporting_text: For calculating the intake of specific carotenoids an additional food composition table has been constructed recently (Goldbohm et al, 1998).

sample_size.excerpt: In the Netherlands Cohort Study among 120 852 subjects aged 55–69 years at baseline (1986), the association between vitamins and carotenoids intake, vitamin supplement use, and bladder cancer incidence was examined.

studies.Authors: Hung RJ, Zhang ZF, Rao JY, Pantuck A, Reuter VE, Heber D, Lu QY

sample_size.excerpt: We performed a case-control study in 242 patients with bladder cancer and 204 healthy controls at Memorial Sloan-Kettering Cancer Center from 1993 to 1997. Epidemiological data and blood specimens were collected on 84 cases and 173 controls.
sample_size.location: abstract; total_n derived from reported group counts 84 + 173 = 257

cases.excerpt: Epidemiological data and blood specimens were collected on 84 cases and 173 controls.

effect_size.excerpt: When using plasma levels of micronutrients as continuous variables, the adjusted OR was 0.22 (95% CI 0.05 to 0.92) for alpha-carotene, 0.42 (95% CI 0.18 to 1.00) for lutein, 0.16 (95% CI 0.02 to 1.06) for zeaxanthin, 0.94 (95% CI 0.89 to 0.99) for lycopene and 0.90 (95% CI 0.81 to 1.00) for beta-cryptoxanthin.
